passage:
Shreya: You've skipped statistics twice this week.
Yusuf: It's so boring. I sit there and my brain shuts.
Shreya: Boring how? Too simple, too tough, or just pointless to you?
Yusuf: Hm. ...The lectures are slow and I already read the chapter. So, too simple?
Shreya: Then maybe you're not lazy. Maybe the boredom is telling you something. Ask ma'am for the harder problem set.
Yusuf: What if she thinks I'm showing off?
Shreya: Say you finished the chapter and want more. That's just true.
Yusuf: ...Okay. And the tutorial part is actually confusing. I'll ask about that too.

qa.q: How many times has Yusuf skipped statistics this week?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What does Yusuf worry about when Shreya suggests asking for the harder problem set?
qa.a: That the teacher will think Yusuf is showing off.

qa.q: What question did Shreya ask that helped, and what did Yusuf decide to do?
qa.a: Shreya asked whether the class was too simple, too tough or pointless. Yusuf saw it was too simple and decided to ask for harder problems.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Yusuf's skipping?
qa.a: Not as laziness but as a signal that something is off with the course, which is why Shreya asks what kind of boring it is.

grounding: A student asks whether boredom in a course means too easy, too hard or meaningless, and reads it as information.

passage:
My name is Avni, and by week five of my economics elective I was drawing spirals in my notebook. Instead of forcing myself to sit up, I wrote three questions on a sticky note: too simple, too tough, or meaningless to me?
The answer came fast: meaningless. I understood every equation but couldn't say who needed them. I told Usha, the teaching assistant, expecting a lecture about discipline. Instead she asked, "What would make it matter to you?"
I said real village data. She pointed me to a project on crop prices. The class didn't change, but I did, and the spirals stopped.

qa.q: What did Avni write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Three questions: too simple, too tough, or meaningless to me?

qa.q: How did Avni feel about the elective by week five, and why?
qa.a: Bored and detached, drawing spirals, because Avni understood the equations but could not say who needed them.

qa.q: What turning point changed the elective for Avni?
qa.a: Usha asked what would make it matter, and Avni chose real village data and a project on crop prices.

qa.q: What might Usha have thought when Avni came to talk?
qa.a: Usha seems to have treated it as a question to solve, not a failure of discipline, so she asked a curious question instead of lecturing.

grounding: A student reads boredom as data by asking whether the course is too easy, too hard or meaningless to them.

passage:
Advisor's notes, 14 September. Student: Siddharth, second-year economics.
Siddharth came in saying he's "bored to death" in Econometrics and wants to drop it. Instead of signing the form straight away, I asked him to sort the boredom. Was the course too easy for him? Was it too hard? Or did it simply mean nothing to him?
He thought for a while. "Not too easy. I get lost in week two and just stop listening." So it's too hard, dressed up as boring. In Microeconomics he says he's bored because it repeats school; that one is too easy.
Plan he proposed: ask the Econometrics tutor for two catch-up sessions, and apply to move into the advanced micro section.
He left looking lighter.
Nandini

qa.q: Which course does Siddharth say repeats school?
qa.a: Microeconomics.

qa.q: What does Siddharth leaving "looking lighter" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt relieved to understand what his boredom meant and to have a plan instead of simply dropping the course.

qa.q: What made Nandini's question useful?
qa.a: Sorting the boredom into too easy, too hard or meaningless showed that Econometrics was too hard and Micro too easy, which need different fixes.

qa.q: What would change if Nandini had simply signed the drop form?
qa.a: Siddharth might have dropped a course he only needed help with, and stayed bored in the one that was too easy.

grounding: Shows a student reading boredom as information, sorting whether a course is too easy, too hard or meaningless.

passage:
Thursday
Third week in a row I've zoned out in Corporate Accounting. Today I caught myself drawing a whole comic in the margins. Naveen nudged me when Ma'am asked me a question and I had no idea.
Tried the test Didi told me about. Is it too easy? Is it too hard? Or does it just not matter to me? Not too easy, I got a B in the quiz. Not too hard, I can do the problems when I try. It's the third one. I don't care about balance sheets. I care about the comic.
That's actually useful to know. Next semester I can pick the design elective instead of Advanced Accounting. And maybe I should ask the career cell whether there's a way to use both.
Ayesha

qa.q: What grade did Ayesha get in the quiz?
qa.a: A B.

qa.q: What does the comic in the margins reveal about how Ayesha feels in class?
qa.a: It shows Ayesha is bored and disengaged in accounting and far more interested in drawing.

qa.q: What did Ayesha learn from the test, and what is the plan?
qa.a: That the boredom means the subject is meaningless to Ayesha, so the plan is to pick the design elective and ask the career cell about using both.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Ayesha zoning out?
qa.a: Naveen noticed and nudged Ayesha, probably worried Ayesha would be caught out by Ma'am again.

grounding: Shows a student using boredom as data, finding a course meaningless to them and using that to guide choices.

passage:
At the agricultural college in the small town, Zubin sat in Farm Machinery class and felt his eyes close. It was the third week in a row.
After class he sat with his friend Hrithik under the neem tree. "I'm so bored in that class. Maybe I'm just lazy."
Hrithik shrugged. "Is it too simple for you? Too tough? Or you just don't care?"
Zubin thought. It wasn't too hard; he'd scored well in the quiz. It wasn't too easy either; he couldn't repair the tractor they practised on. "I think I don't see why I'd ever use it. I want to work on seeds and soil, not engines."
"So that's not lazy. That's information."
Zubin looked at the elective list that evening. Seed Science had space. He switched the next week, and stayed awake for every class.

qa.q: Which elective did Zubin switch to?
qa.a: Zubin switched to Seed Science.

qa.q: What was Zubin worried about when he said he might be lazy?
qa.a: Zubin felt anxious and ashamed that his boredom meant a flaw in him rather than a mismatch with the course.

qa.q: What question helped Zubin, and why?
qa.a: Hrithik asked whether the class was too easy, too hard or meaningless to him, which turned boredom into information that guided his choice.

qa.q: How did Hrithik see Zubin's boredom?
qa.a: Hrithik didn't judge it as laziness; he saw it as a useful signal worth reading.

grounding: A student reads his boredom in a course as data, asks whether it is too easy, too hard or meaningless, and chooses better.
